newsitem.title: UK: Australian reinsurers drive into world markets.
newsitem.headline: Australian reinsurers drive into world markets.

text.p: Australian reinsurers, driven by their own expansion and the lure of their home market for foreign groups, are increasingly making their presence felt in international markets.

In the last year they have built up their international business. At the same time, Australia's own reinsurance market is attracting other major international reinsurers, many of them seeking an entry point for Asia.
Australia's reinsurance companies -- GIO Re, Reinsurance Australia Corp (ReAC) and Sydney Re (trading as QBE International in London) -- are all making strides across the globe.

QBE this week announced higher first-quarter net profits, boosted by strong growth in reinsurance business, which it expects to increase by 10-20 percent in the current year, bolstered by its recent acquisition of Allstate Re.

The deal, to be completed next month, will build QBE's London operations and provide access to business it would not previously have seen. It also means that around 55 percent of QBE's business will come from overseas.

ReAC has also improved its performance. The company only started underwriting reinsurance in November 1993 but by 1994 it had already reached number 93 in Standard & Poor's top 100 reinsurers. ReAC's net premium for 1995 was A$314 million, almost double 1994's figure.
This should grow in 1996 following the opening of an underwriting office in Nice to access markets in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

GIO Re, another relative newcomer to reinsurance, which wrote its first contracts in 1986 when it was part of the Government Insurance Office of New South Wales, has shown similar ambition and is currently ranked at 32 in Standard & Poor's top 100.
Earlier this month it, too, reported a significant improvement from reinsurance activities.
Australia's proximity to Southeast Asia means it is attracting the attention of other international reinsurers and Sydney is shaping up to be a stepping stone into Asia.
Some industry analysts have even likened Sydney's potential as an insurance centre to Bermuda, which burst onto the scene during 1993 and 1994 with fresh capital.
Bermuda took advantage of problems at Lloyd's of London and other reinsurance centres to grab a hefty share of the market

Global reinsurers are flocking to reinsure Australia's insurance companies and about 20 foreign groups have set up there. International giants such as Munich Re and Swiss Re have in the past six months been joined by NAC Re, Rhine Re and Employers Re.
Other applications from offshore players are pending and a new local reinsurer, New Cap Re, is being set up with the support of Australian institutions and U.S. capital.

Growth in reinsurance is outstripping expansion in primary insurance and, although Australia accounts for only four to five percent of world reinsurance premiums, it is enough to attract global players keen to diversify their business.

The Australian domestic market has also offered reinsurers steady profits. It tends to still follow the British market but because there have been no catastrophes of any significance since the Newcastle (New South Wales) earthquake in 1991, reinsurers have had a profitable period for three to four years.
However, those margins may soon come under pressure as the market is over-serviced and catastrophe rates now come under pressure from underwriters in Bermuda, analysts say.

As in other countries, lawyers have warned that the growth of consumerism in Australia will continue to make people better educated about their rights, leading to an increase in claims and litigation, particularly as the government and consumer associations develop legislation to protect policyholders.

There have also been suggestions that European and U.S. insurers might use developments such as Internet distribution to undercut Australian rivals, getting around traditional obstacles that have stopped them accessing the sophisticated market.

Australian reinsurers are confident that overseas business will help offset any decline at home. And even if foreign reinsurers do not quite see Sydney as a "new Bermuda", it looks set to remain an important base for their drive into the East.
-- Gordon Mackenzie, Reuters Insurance News 44 171 542 2770
